passage: The crying had gone quiet in the flat in Buenos Aires. Valentina, five, peeped out from behind the curtain. Her papá, Andrés, was on the sofa folding laundry, not looking cross. Her throat still hurt from yelling at him about the dulce de leche. She shuffled over, stopped, then climbed into his lap and hid her face in his shirt. "I said bad words," she whispered. Andrés wrapped both arms around her. "You were very angry. I still love you, all the way." Valentina's body went soft and heavy. She kept her face hidden, but she held on.

qa.q: What was Andrés doing on the sofa?
qa.a: He was on the sofa folding laundry, not looking cross.

qa.q: What does Valentina hiding her face in his shirt suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems ashamed of the bad words and relieved to be held 🤍; hiding her face shows the shame, while holding on shows she needs to know they're still close.

qa.q: What did Andrés say that helped at this stage, and why?
qa.a: He named her anger and said he still loved her "all the way", which tells her the bond survived her outburst.

qa.q: What might Andrés be feeling as Valentina climbs into his lap?
qa.a: He is probably relieved the storm has passed and tender toward her, glad she came back to him on her own.

grounding: After crying, a five-year-old girl climbs into her father's lap, ashamed and relieved, and hears that her anger did not make her unlovable.

passage: The community centre hall smelled of floor polish after dance class. Preeti, five, had wailed by the shoe rack because her father said no to a second laddoo from the snack table. Now she sat on the bench, hiccupping. Jagdish sat at the far end, waiting. Slowly Preeti slid along the bench, bit by bit, until she was against his arm. Then she crawled into his lap. "Are you still my papa?" she mumbled into his kurta. "Always," Jagdish said, rocking her a little. "Even when you're angry." Her fingers curled into his sleeve.

qa.q: Where had Preeti wailed?
qa.a: Preeti had wailed by the shoe rack.

qa.q: What worry is behind Preeti's question "Are you still my papa?"
qa.a: She seems afraid that her anger may have broken their closeness, so she needs to hear she is still loved.

qa.q: Why was waiting at the far end of the bench a good choice for Jagdish?
qa.a: It let Preeti cool down at her own pace and come to him when ready, so the reconnection felt safe and was her own choice.

qa.q: What might Jagdish feel as her fingers curl into his sleeve?
qa.a: Likely relief and warmth, knowing the hard moment is over and his daughter still trusts him.

grounding: A young girl, after a tantrum over a sweet, slides into her father's lap needing to know that her anger has not broken the bond.

passage:
Creche note for home, Tuesday
Chinnu cried hard at pickup because the snack tin was closed. Her papa, Jeevan, kept the no calmly. When the crying slowed, she walked over and climbed into his lap, face pressed to his shirt. She whispered, "Are you still my papa?" I think she was worried the shouting had spoiled something. Jeevan said, "Always. Even when you're cross." Her shoulders came down and she held his thumb. They sat like that until the rickshaw came. Tomorrow I will read the storybook about angry feelings at circle time.
Samir, creche caregiver

qa.q: What did Chinnu whisper to Jeevan?
qa.a: "Are you still my papa?"

qa.q: What does Chinnu's whisper suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems ashamed and scared that her shouting had spoiled things with her papa, then relieved when he said "Always."

qa.q: How could Samir support Chinnu tomorrow at creche?
qa.a: By reading the story about angry feelings, helping her learn that big feelings are allowed and do not stop people caring.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan when Chinnu climbs into his lap?
qa.a: He likely feels tender and relieved that the crying is over, and wants her to know the bond is still safe.

grounding: Shows a young girl, after crying, climbing into her father's lap, needing to hear that her anger did not break their bond.

passage:
The evening light was going orange over the fields when Chutki finally stopped crying. She had screamed at Abbu that she hated him, all over a gur ladoo, and now she sat in the doorway of the hut hugging her knees.
Rafiq was mending a rope on the charpai. He patted the space beside him and said nothing.
Chutki came slowly. She climbed into his lap and hid her face.
"I said a bad thing," she mumbled.
"You were very angry," Rafiq said. "I still love you the same."
From the kitchen, Kavitha watched her daughter's small fists uncurl.

qa.q: What was Rafiq mending?
qa.a: A rope on the charpai.

qa.q: What was Chutki feeling when she mumbled "I said a bad thing"?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of shouting that she hated Abbu and worried he might not love her, and his answer relieved her.

qa.q: What small step helped Chutki come back to Rafiq?
qa.a: He quietly patted the space beside him without a lecture, so she could come when ready.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel watching from the kitchen?
qa.a: She is likely relieved and moved to see Chutki's fists uncurl in her father's lap.

grounding: Shows a young girl in a village climbing into her father's lap after crying, ashamed, and hearing she is still loved.

passage:
In the small Lisbon flat, Leila had cried on the hallway floor for a long time about the chocolate egg. Now it was quiet.
Her dad, Tomás, sat on the sofa with a book he wasn't reading. Leila padded in, red-eyed, and climbed onto his lap without a word. She tucked her head under his chin.
"I shouted at you," she said into his jumper.
"You did. And I love you exactly the same."
She let out a huge shaky breath.
In the doorway, her mum, Beatriz, smiled and went to put the kettle on.

qa.q: Who was sitting on the sofa with a book?
qa.a: Her dad, Tomás, with a book he wasn't reading.

qa.q: What does Leila's huge shaky breath suggest?
qa.a: She felt relieved after being ashamed and unsure whether her shouting had changed how her dad felt about her.

qa.q: Which of Tomás's words helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saying he loved her exactly the same, because it told her that her anger had not made her unlovable.

qa.q: How does Beatriz seem to feel watching from the doorway?
qa.a: Beatriz looks relieved and warm, smiling because the storm is over and the two of them are close again.

grounding: Shows a young girl abroad climbing into her father's lap after crying and learning her shouting did not break the bond.

passage: At the community centre playgroup, Sabina had cried and shouted for ten minutes because her painted kite had to stay until it dried. Now she was quiet, hiccupping. Abbu, who had come to fetch her, sat on the low bench. Sabina edged closer, peeking at him, then climbed into his lap and hid her face in his shirt. "I said you're a bad Abbu," she whispered. "Am I still your Sabina?" Abbu held her close. "Always. Even when you're angry." Sabina's shoulders dropped. Jahnavi Ma'am, packing away paints, smiled. "The kite will be dry tomorrow, Sabina."

qa.q: Why did Sabina's painted kite have to stay at the playgroup?
qa.a: It had to stay until it dried.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel as she hid her face in Abbu's shirt?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of calling him a bad Abbu and relieved to be held, needing to know she was still loved.

qa.q: Why was Abbu's answer the right one at this stage?
qa.a: By saying 'Always. Even when you're angry', he showed her that her anger had not broken their bond.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi Ma'am feel watching them?
qa.a: Jahnavi Ma'am seems warm and pleased to see Sabina comforted, and adds a reassuring word about the kite.

grounding: Shows a child after a tantrum climbing into her father's lap, ashamed and relieved, needing to know she is still loved.
